chunks: He is the One whose punishment on His enemies is harsh despite the extent of His Mercy,
and His compassion for His friends is vast despite His harsh punishment.
He overpowers one who wants to overcome Him, and destroys one who clashes with Him. He disgraces one who opposes Him and gains sway over one who bears Him hostility.
He is sufficient for one who relies on Him. He gives one who asks Him. He repays one who lends to Him. He rewards one who thanks Him.
ai.seo_question: How does God's mercy coexist with His punishment according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) articulates the dialectic of divine justice and mercy, illustrating how God's overwhelming power (Qahr) for His enemies is the very foundation of His expansive mercy (Rahma) for His friends. This reflects the Shia theological understanding that God's attributes are not contradictory but complementary, where His dominance over the rebellious ensures the security and elevation of the faithful. The text further emphasizes the reciprocal nature of the believer's relationship with God, linking trust (Tawakkul), supplication, and gratitude to divine sufficiency and reward.
